parsed_answer.content:
Tuning the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is a trade-off between throughput and latency, governed by the physics of Garbage Collection (GC). High-throughput applications, such as batch processing or data transformation pipelines, prioritize the total volume of work completed over a given period, often tolerating longer 'stop-the-world' (STW) pauses to maximize CPU efficiency. In contrast, low-latency applications—like high-frequency trading platforms or real-time user interfaces—prioritize consistent, sub-millisecond response times, requiring the JVM to perform GC work concurrently with application threads, which inevitably consumes more CPU cycles and reduces total throughput.

To achieve high throughput, we typically leverage the Parallel GC (UseParallelGC), which utilizes multiple threads to perform young and old generation collections, minimizing the overhead of GC management at the cost of freezing application threads. For low-latency requirements, we shift to concurrent collectors like G1 (Garbage First) or ZGC (Z Garbage Collector). These collectors trade off total throughput by offloading marking and compaction phases to background threads, ensuring that the application remains responsive even under heavy allocation pressure.

items: High-throughput tuning often involves setting -XX:+UseParallelGC and adjusting -XX:ParallelGCThreads to match physical core counts, allowing the JVM to saturate the CPU during collection cycles.

Low-latency tuning relies on ZGC or Shenandoah, which use colored pointers and load barriers to perform heap compaction concurrently, effectively eliminating the need for long STW pauses regardless of heap size.

Memory allocation rate is the silent killer; in low-latency systems, you must monitor the 'Allocation Rate' vs. 'Promotion Rate' to ensure the young generation doesn't overflow into the old generation prematurely, causing expensive Major GCs.
For G1GC, tuning -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis sets a soft target for the collector; setting this too low forces the JVM to perform more frequent, smaller collections, which can ironically degrade throughput.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap is 'over-tuning.' Engineers often set -Xms and -Xmx to the same value to avoid heap resizing overhead, but if you don't account for native memory (Metaspace/CodeCache), you risk OOM-Killer termination by the OS. Always profile your application's 'live set' size under peak load before fixing the heap size; if your heap is too large, you increase the time it takes to scan the object graph, which can actually increase latency in non-concurrent collectors.

title: How do you tune the JVM for a high-throughput vs a low-latency application?
